In The Gambia, tensions between farmers and herders in Central River Region South (CRR-S), Central River Region North (CRR-N), North Bank Region (NBR), and Lower River Region (LRR) have intensified 
due to climate change, environmental degradation, and rising socio-economic pressures, increasing competition over land and water resources.
Transhumance remains a key livelihood strategy but increasing resource scarcity and cross-border livestock movements between The Gambia and Senegal continue to heighten pressure on host communities.
Through its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), IOM developed the Transhumance Tracking Tool (TTT) to monitor transhumance movements and related vulnerabilities in the four regions and to support 
peaceful transhumance practices.
Over the five-month period from November 2025 to March 2026, the TTT early warning system captured 151 alerts through trained enumerators, key informants, community representatives, and local 
authorities. These included movement-related alerts (66%) and sudden events (34%), helping stakeholders identify risks, inform timely responses, and support conflict prevention.

Over the five-month period from November 2025 to March 2026, movement alerts indicated that 58 per cent of reported movements were categorized as mass movements, 27 per cent as late movements, 
14 per cent as early movements, and 1 per cent as other types of movement, such as seasonal movements. Reported transhumance movements took place across regions in The Gambia and Senegal.
All key informants (100%) indicated that the reported movement alerts had the potential to result in agro-pastoral conflict. In addition, 75 per cent of respondents assessed the probability of risk 
materialization as likely, 21 per cent as very likely, and 4 per cent as unlikely.
Event alerts showed that 27 per cent related to agro-pastoral conflict, 29 per cent to farmer–herder conflicts, 27 per cent to disasters, and 10 per cent to inter-community tensions. The main reported causes 
of agro-pastoral conflict were grazing area encroachment (27%), farmland encroachment (17%), damage to surrounding fields by pastoral groups (13%), and the early or late movement of pastoral groups 
(6%), with other causes accounting for 10 per cent. The main actors involved in event alerts were national and/or local authorities (29%), local farmers and breeders (29%), pastoral groups in transhumance 
(23%), and others (12%).
Key actors involved in conflict management included community leaders (89%), village committees (72%), local and/or national authorities (61%), religious leaders (50%), farmers (44%), other actors (44%), 
herders (28%), and pastoral organizations (22%). In terms of outcomes, 35 per cent of reported events were resolved, 62 per cent remained unresolved, and 4 per cent were reported as unknown.

31,276In The Gambia, following the transmission of alerts by key informants in CRR South, CRR North, North Bank Region, and Lower River Region, a range of actions was undertaken by local actors to support 
conflict prevention and resolution. These responses were implemented both to address situations identified through event alerts and to prevent imminent inter-community tensions associated with movement 
alerts. Depending on the nature of the alert, some measures were taken to prevent, mitigate, or resolve tensions linked to transhumance movements. Other reported incidents, not directly related to 
transhumance, also prompted local responses, including farmer–herder clashes and property damage. The examples highlighted below illustrate some of the actions taken to document and respond to 
reported alerts.

In The Gambia, community leaders and Village Communities played an active role in resolving conflicts reported through alerts. Pastoralist groups and farming communities, in coordination with local authorities 
and Religion leaders, also contributed to addressing reported disputes and managing anticipated livestock movements. Their involvement supported community-based solutions aimed at reducing tensions and 
promoting peaceful transhumance.

The opinions expressed in the report are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the International Organization for Migration (IOM). The designations employed and the presentation of material 
throughout the report do not imply the expression of any opinion whatsoever on the part of IOM concerning the legal status of any country, territory, city, or area, or of its authorities, or concerning its frontiers or boundaries. 
IOM is committed to the principle that humane and orderly migration benefits migrants and society. As an intergovernmental organization, IOM acts with its partners in the international community to assist in the meeting 
of operational challenges of migration; advance understanding of migration issues; to encourage social and economic development through migration; and to uphold the human dignity and well-being of migrants.

related.excerpt: One of CIA’s oldest and most recognizable intelligence publications, The World Factbook, has sunset. The World Factbook served the Intelligence Community and the general public as a longstanding, one-stop basic reference about countries and communities around the globe. Let’s take a quick look into the history of The World Factbook. Over many decades, The World Factbook evolved from a classified to unclassified, hardcopy to electronic product that added new categories, and even new global entities. The original classified publication, titled The National Basic Intelligence Factbook, launched in 1962. The first unclassified companion version was issued in 1971. A decade later it was renamed The World Factbook. In 1997, The World Factbook went digital and debuted to a worldwide audience on CIA.gov, where it garnered millions of views each year. related.summary: The UN agency said that following the agreed MoU and reopening of the strait, global oil supply rose by 4.1 million bpd in June, although supply remained 9.4 million bpd below pre-war levels. The return of fighting between the United States and Iran threatens to extend the global energy crisis, the International Energy Agency has warned.
bullets: The UN agency said that following the agreed MoU and reopening of the strait, global oil supply rose by 4.1 million bpd in June, although supply remained 9.4 million bpd below pre-war levels.
The return of fighting between the United States and Iran threatens to extend the global energy crisis, the International Energy Agency has warned.

Recommended Stories list of 3 items end of list The warning came as a lull in action from US and Iranian forces appeared to pave the way for efforts to revive diplomacy, although sources cautioned that the US military remains ready to resume attacks.
The IEA reported that the effective closure of Hormuz had cut as much as 14 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil flows.
Analysts said the relative calm reflected market confidence that the situation would stabilise, even as tightening inventories point to further upward pressure on prices in the coming weeks.
related.excerpt: The return of fighting between the United States and Iran threatens to extend the global energy crisis, the International Energy Agency has warned. The risk that the resumption of hostilities could scupper hopes of a swift recovery in energy markets was flagged by the United Nations agency on Friday. Recommended Stories list of 3 items end of list The warning came as a lull in action from US and Iranian forces appeared to pave the way for efforts to revive diplomacy, although sources cautioned that the US military remains ready to resume attacks. World oil demand is on track to fall this year for the first time since 2020, the IEA said in its latest monthly oil market report, as the conflict continues to disrupt production and exports across the Middle East. A recovery had been under way on the strength of last month’s US-Iran memorandum of understanding, the agency said, but it cautioned that renewed escalation could complicate the outlook further. The latest round of fighting this week was triggered by rival interpretations of provisions governing the Strait of Hormuz in the MoU.
